title: Oklahoma City bombing
description: 1995 domestic terrorist attack in Oklahoma, US
wiki_lead:
On April 19, 1995, American anti-government extremist Timothy McVeigh, assisted by Terry Nichols, detonated a makeshift bomb stored in a rental truck parked in front of the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, in an act of domestic terrorism. The explosion killed 167 people, injured 684, and destroyed more than a third of the building. The attack also destroyed or damaged 324 other buildings, destroyed 86 vehicles, and caused an estimated $652 million in damage. During rescue operations after the bombing, a rescue worker was killed after being struck on the head by falling debris, bringing the total death toll to 168.
Within 90 minutes of the explosion, McVeigh was stopped by Oklahoma Highway Patrolman Charlie Hanger for driving without a license plate and was arrested for illegal weapons possession. Forensic evidence quickly linked McVeigh and Nichols to the attack; within days, both men were charged. Michael and Lori Fortier were later identified as accomplices. McVeigh, a combat veteran of the Gulf War, had rented a Ryder truck, which he later filled with the explosives used in the attack. Nichols assisted McVeigh in planning the attack and making the bomb. 
McVeigh and Nichols were primarily motivated by their anger at the U.S. federal government, particularly its handling of the law enforcement sieges at Ruby Ridge in 1992 and Waco in 1993, as well as the 1994 Federal Assault Weapons Ban. McVeigh had timed the retaliatory attack to coincide with the second anniversary of the end of the siege in Waco and the Battles of Lexington and Concord, the first engagements of the American Revolutionary War.
The official Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) report on the bombing, referred to as "OKBOMB", involved 28,000 interviews, 7,100 lbs (3,200 kg) of evidence, and nearly one billion pieces of information. When the FBI raided McVeigh's home, they found a telephone number that led them to a farm where McVeigh had purchased supplies for the bombing. The bombers were tried and convicted in 1997. McVeigh was sentenced to death and was executed via lethal injection on June 11, 2001, at the U.S. federal penitentiary in Terre Haute, Indiana. Nichols was sentenced to life in prison without the possibility of parole. 
In response to the bombing, the U.S. Congress passed the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996, which limited access to habeas corpus in the United States, among other provisions. It also passed legislation to increase the protection around federal buildings, to deter future terrorist attacks. The bombing remains the deadliest act of domestic terrorism in U.S. history, and was the deadliest terrorist attack in U.S. history until the September 11 attacks.

grok_lead: The Oklahoma City bombing was a domestic terrorist attack on April 19, 1995. Timothy McVeigh detonated a truck bomb outside the Alfred P. Murrah Federal Building in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma. It killed 168 people, including 19 children, and injured more than 680 others. McVeigh, a U.S. Army Gulf War veteran who resented the federal government, targeted the site. It housed agencies such as the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms (ATF) and Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA). He blamed them for the Waco siege and Ruby Ridge standoff. Terry Nichols, another opponent of the government, helped McVeigh get and mix bomb parts. These included ammonium nitrate fertilizer, nitromethane, and diesel fuel. McVeigh rented a Ryder truck. He loaded it with about 5,000 pounds of explosives. He parked it at the building's north entrance. He set time-delay fuses and walked away. The blast hit at 9:02 a.m. It wrecked one-third of the nine-story building. It also damaged more than 300 nearby structures. The explosion was the worst domestic terrorism in U.S. history before September 11, 2001. Rescue teams worked right away through rubble of concrete and steel. Investigators tied debris to McVeigh. This included the truck 's axle and its vehicle identification number. Police arrested him 90 minutes later in a traffic stop. In 1997, a court found McVeigh guilty of federal murder and conspiracy. He received a death sentence. Officials executed him by lethal injection on June 11, 2001. A court convicted Nichols of conspiracy and manslaughter. He got life imprisonment without parole. Witnesses described unknown suspects like " John Doe 2." This led to questions about other helpers. Official probes ruled these claims baseless. The bombing spurred new laws. One was the Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996. It sped up federal habeas corpus reviews. It raised punishments for terrorism. The attack exposed risks in federal buildings. It drew attention to U.S. extremism rooted in anger at government actions.
